title: Queen-Raid Gambits
subtitle: Blackburne–Shilling and Stafford: greed meets checkmate.
goals: Execute the Stafford Gambit's main trap
Learn the greed-detector: why Nxe5 loses

steps.say: Joseph Blackburne allegedly played this for shilling stakes in London pubs: 3...Nd4?! dangles the e5 pawn, and White just took it with 4.Nxe5??. Now the queen raid begins — and it ends with a picture-perfect smothered-style mate ON WHITE'S OWN BACK RANK. Seven forced moves. You're Black; make it cost more than a shilling.

steps.prompt: White grabbed the poisoned e5 pawn. Launch the queen raid — seven moves ending in mate!
hints: Qg5! forks the loose e5 knight and the g2 pawn — White can't hold both, and grabbing f7 makes it worse.
After Nxf7 Qxg2, Rf1, the killer geometry: Qxe4+ hits king AND then your d4 knight lands on f3 — mate with three white pieces watching helplessly.

line.say: The double attack: the e5 knight hangs, g2 hangs behind it. White's 'best try' is the counter-raid on f7...
Ignore the fork on your own queen and rook — the g2 capture threatens mate on e4/g1 lines already...
Check — and the e4 queen now eyes the same light squares as your d4 knight. White's only block...

MATE — the d4 knight's only good move of the game is the last move of the game. King boxed by his own bishop, rook and pawns; Blackburne collects his shilling. Note White's knight sits on f7 'winning' your rook: material means nothing to a mated king.

rejections.say: The knight slinks home and White keeps a clean extra pawn. ...Nd4 was never about safety — it was bait, and the hook is the queen raid: Qg5!
The right spirit, wrong square — g3! blunts it and White keeps the pawn. From g5 the queen forks e5 AND g2: geometry is everything in a raid.

steps.wrongSay: Two loose White targets sit on one queen move's crosshairs: the e5 knight and the g2 pawn.
steps.successSay: The Blackburne–Shilling trap: seven moves, one shilling, checkmate. Greed on e5 has never recovered.

steps.prompt: The Stafford Gambit — internet-famous for exactly this position. White's 6.Bg5?? pins your knight... doesn't it? Play the punishment: five moves to mate!
hints: The 'pin' is fake for the same reason as every fake pin: a big enough counter-blow. Your knight can jump — check what Bxd8 costs White.
Nxe4!! — and when White grabs the queen with Bxd8, the machine runs: Bxf2+, Ke2, Bg4#.

line.say: The fake pin is called. If White plays dxe4, then ...Bxg5 regains everything with a better game — so White grabs the queen...
The counter-operation begins with check. Kxf2 loses to ...Nxg5+ picking everything up, so the king steps aside...

MATE ON MOVE EIGHT. Both bishops and the e4 knight weave the net: f2-bishop seals the dark squares, g4-bishop checks, the knight covers the rest. White 'won a queen' and lost the game — the Stafford's most famous line.

rejections.say: Bxf6 Qxf6 and White is simply better — a pawn up, no attack. The Stafford lives on the fake-pin break: Nxe4!!
Spirited — but one move early: Kxf2! and there's no follow-up, the bishop is just gone. The knight jump comes FIRST: Nxe4! opens the queen's defense of g5 and loads everything.

steps.wrongSay: Every Stafford player waits their whole life for this position. The knight is NOT really pinned.
steps.successSay: Nxe4!! Bxd8 Bxf2+ Ke2 Bg4# — the trap that made the Stafford famous. And the meta-lesson of this whole topic: pins against queens are suggestions, not laws.

steps.say: Defending against these raids is one habit: BEFORE grabbing any early pawn, ask what recaptures and what attacks follow. Against Blackburne–Shilling, simply castle or play c3 — the d4 knight retreats in shame. Against the Stafford, play d3 and h3 early and never touch g5 with the bishop. Free pawns in move-4 positions are almost always rented, not owned.
